title-group.article-title: Uncovering the genetic basis of Staphylococcusaureus resistance to single antimicrobial peptides and their combinations

abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, prompting the exploration of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) as alternatives. Here, we investigated the genetic mechanisms of resistance evolution in Staphylococcus aureus against single and combined AMPs (temporin, melittin, and pexiganan). Whole-genome sequencing of evolved populations revealed that combination therapy significantly reduced the overall number of mutations, and importantly, did not typically lead to broad multi-AMP resistance. Instead, resistance likely focused on one component of the combination. While mutations in pmtR (toxin transport) and tagO (wall-teichoic acid biosynthesis) were common across treatments, AMP-specific mutations, such as dagK and msrR, were also identified. Notably, mutations in a hypothetical membrane protein operon (SAOUHSC_02307–02309) imply a potential pexiganan resistance pathway. The findings suggest that AMP combinations might limit mutation accumulation, while constraining the development of general AMP resistance. The genetic mechanism of resistance is complex, thus careful selection is required for designing effective AMP-based therapies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as a critical global health challenge, with antibiotic-resistant bacterial pathogens posing a significant threat to human lives.1,2 The rise in mortality rates attributed to AMR pathogens, coupled with the increasing diversity of resistant populations, emphasizes the urgent need for innovative approaches for combating pathogens. One promising direction is using antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) as alternative therapeutic agents. AMPs, which are known for their versatile mechanism of action, primarily through interactions with the bacterial membrane, are naturally produced by all three domains of life.3,4,5 Another potential advantage of AMP treatment is that previous studies found that resistance to AMPs evolved slowly and to a lesser extent than to antibiotics.6,7,8,9 However, resistance to AMPs has been observed both in natural and laboratory settings.10 A different approach to combat the expanding AMR phenomenon is by using combination therapy. Combination therapy can include the simultaneous application of antimicrobials, but also different forms of sequential use of different drugs. This approach is well-known and widely used, especially in clinical settings. Combination therapy offers several advantages, such as enhanced bactericidal effect, lowered dosage requirement, eradication of biofilms, and prevention of drug resistance.11,12,13,14 Previous research has been conducted to elucidate the genetic basis of AMP resistance.10,15 In gram-negative bacteria, resistance primarily arises from modifications in bacterial membrane structures, such as LPS and phospholipids, as well as through biofilm formation, efflux pump utilization, and protease production.16 Similarly, gram-positive bacteria adapt by adjusting the cell wall and membrane to reduce the outer negative charge, in addition to employing efflux pumps and proteases to export and degrade the AMPs.17 Specifically, Staphylococcus bacteria use a two-component graRS system for sensing and responding to AMPs.18 This system activates the expression of various genes that control AMP resistance. One such operon is the dlt operon, which integrates D-alanine amino acid into the cell wall teichoic acid (WTA). Another gene regulated by graRS is mprF, which produces lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG). Both contribute to reducing the negative charge of the membrane to prevent AMP action. In addition, it controls the ABC transporter encoded by vraFG, which is associated with AMP resistance.19 In the case of Staphylococcus aureus, genetic signatures of AMP-evolved populations have been described in few studies.20,21 However, our understanding of the genetic mechanisms causing resistance to AMPs, particularly in combination, is very limited. In a previous study, we selected three well-characterized AMPs that also showed medium to high resistance in a preliminary experiment, and evolved S. aureus with these single AMPs and their combinations.22 We found that some combinations of two AMPs exhibited a significant ability to delay the evolution of resistance and the resulting change in MIC was lower for combinations than single AMPs in most cases. In the current study, we aimed to reveal the genetic profiles of these evolved populations to gain insight into the genetic mechanisms behind the development of resistance and the trajectories that led to the emergence of unique genetic profiles. Specifically, we address the following questions: (1) Are combinations likely to affect mutation occurrence? (2) Do combination-evolved populations utilize the same resistance mechanisms as those that arise in response to individual AMPs, or do they employ novel pathways? (3) Do populations evolved with combinations exhibit greater genomic and phenotypic diversity compared to those exposed to individual AMPs? Our findings will provide a crucial basis for the design of effective and resilient AMP cocktails, which have the potential to be a significant advancement in combating antibiotic-resistant bacterial pathogens while also lowering the risk of drug resistance evolution.

sec.title: The combination of AMPs significantly reduced the amount of observed mutations, particularly within Pex-Mel combination
sec.p:
In our previous work, we have evolved the opportunistic pathogen Staphylococcus aureus in the presence of three single AMPs (temporin-Temp; melittin-Mel; pexiganan-Pex) and their combinations (Figure 1A).22 Briefly, we exposed the bacteria to different concentrations of AMPs according to their MIC values, and gradually increased the AMP concentrations in response to changes in the populations’ MICs throughout the experiment. We evolved six parallel evolutionary replicates under each treatment (AMP/AMP-combination) for 29 days. After the experiment, the evolved populations were frozen in a glycerol stock (−80°C). Subsequently, all 36 evolving bacterial populations were regrown, characterized for antimicrobial sensitivity and fitness costs of resistance, and their genomic DNA was extracted and sequenced. Since we were interested in mutations that are likely to contribute to increased resistance to AMPs in our experimentally evolved populations, we excluded the synonymous mutations, and mutations that occurred in the control populations that evolve in the absence of AMPs (NPSA). Across nine different control populations, we identified 26 mutations, with the most frequent being a point mutation in agrA at the same position, suggesting it originated during the pre-experiment habituation stage (Figure S1).Figure 1
The number of mutations per population is reduced under AMP combination treatment
(A) Experimental settings. S. aureus bacteria evolved with different AMPs and AMP combinations through 29 days (approximately 122 generations). The bacterial genomic DNA was then extracted from each population and whole-genome sequencing subsequently performed.
(B) The number of mutations per population among different treatments. Statistical analysis performed using post-hoc Dunn’s test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Boxes represent the interquartile range (IQR) results, middle line indicates the median, whiskers represent 1.5∗IQR, and dots represent each population.
(C) The number of mutations per population between single AMP and AMP combination treatment. Statistical analysis performed using Mann-Whitney U test. Colored dots identify the populations from different treatments. Mutations shown in B and C exclude synonymous mutations and mutations present in the control strain (NPSA). Mutation data for the control strain is presented in Figure S1.

After this filtration, we found 149 mutations within 66 different genes in 36 evolved populations. Out of the most frequent mutations (frequency > 3) single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were the majority (59), followed by deletion mutations (18), and insertions (5) (Figure S2). Intriguingly, 25 SNPs were nonsense, i.e., led to stop codon (42.4%). Additionally, over 50% of the common mutations observed were either nonsense, insertions, or deletions, which are more prone to cause protein dysfunction. In single AMP populations, Mel populations (i.e., the evolutionary replicates which evolved in the presence of the AMP Melittin) exhibited a significantly higher number of mutations per strain compared with Temp populations (Figure 1B; mean of 6.5 vs. 3; Dunn’s test, p = 0.035). In the combination treatment, Pex-Mel treatment notably decreased the number of mutations per population (means of 6.5, 6, and 2 mutations per Mel, Pex, and Pex-Mel, respectively; Dunn’s test, pMel = 0.004, pPex = 0.013). The other combination treatments also showed a trend toward a lower number of mutations; however, these differences were not statistically significant. Overall comparison between single and combination treatments identified a significantly lower number of mutations per population in the combinations (Figure 1C; Table S1; mean of 5.2 vs. 3.1; two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.005).

Moreover, the number of mutations per population was correlated with the level of resistance (Figure 2; Pearson correlation, r = 0.672, p < 0.0001). Taken together, these findings indicate that the resistance mechanism to AMPs is intricate, involving several mutations, while more mutations within the population will likely result in higher resistance.Figure 2
Mutation-resistance correlation
Every dot in the figure represents a population. The MIC fold change of the combinations calculated as the average of the two AMPs MIC fold-change. Trend line represents the linear regression, as the confidence interval represented in gray color around the line. Pearson coefficient and p value are presented.

sec.title: S. aureus evolved both mutations that arose in multiple AMP treatments as well as treatment-specific ones
sec.p:
Within the single-AMP evolved populations, the most frequent gene in which mutations occurred was pmtR (13/36 populations, Figure 3). The protein PmtR is a DNA-binding repressor from the ytrA family, which inhibits the transcription of the phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) toxins transporter genes (pmt) in S. aureus.23 Interestingly, all of the mutations were SNPs that led to stop-codon in the fifth amino acid, except for Temp2 population (Gly73Glu) (Figure S2). The second most prevalent mutations appeared in tagO, which evolved across all treatments except for Temp. The TagO protein is involved in the wall-teichoic acid biosynthesis.24 Other abundant mutations were identified in rpoB, agrA, and graS genes, which evolved in Mel and Pex populations. Notably, all graS mutations possessed agrA, rpoB, and pmtR mutations (4/4). rpoB, responsible for the beta subunit of the RNA polymerase, is found to have mutations in most Mel populations (5/6) and only in two Pex populations. GraS is a two-component regulatory system kinase sensor, known to be involved in AMR,25 while AgrA is a regulatory sensor of another quorum sensing system—the accessory gene regulatory (agr),26 which regulates a variety of virulence attributes. It is particularly noteworthy that all of these mutations in both agrA and graS were deletion mutations (Figure S2).Figure 3
The frequency of mutations across different treatments and genes
The figure presents the mutations that evolved in more than 3 populations. The colored cells identify mutations that appeared in at least three populations within the same single AMP treatment but not in other single AMPs. Mutations that were significant to one treatment in Fisher’s-exact test were also colored (see statistical analysis in supplemental information). Gray colors indicate mutations that were not specific to a certain AMP treatment, or not statistically significant.

While the mutations mentioned previously occurred across two or more treatments, we found a few mutations that were associated with a specific AMP. Within temporin populations, the most notable mutations were found in dagK (also known as dgkB) in four out of six populations (Figure 3; Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, p = 0.016). dagK encodes a diacylglycerol kinase which phosphorylates diacylglycerol into phosphatidic acid.27 Notably, the mutations occurred in conserved regions (Pro11Ser, Thr70Ile, and Met128Ile), potentially leading to a reduction in the catalytic activity.27 Interestingly, all dagK mutants had collateral sensitivity to pexiganan (Figure S5; Point-biserial correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, rpb = −0.59, p = 0.009). An additional gene that mutated in Temp populations was mnhA1 (3/6, Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, p = 0.024). This gene is transcribed into a subunit of the cation/proton antiporter Mnh1, which facilitates the survival of S. aureus in extreme conditions.28 glpF and glpK evolved in two Temp populations each, suggesting that GlpFK might be involved in the activity of temporin. GlpFK facilitates the uptake of glycerol, which can then be converted into phospholipids in the membrane.29 In the presence of Melittin msrR mutations were evolved in five out of six evolutionary replicates (Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, p = 0.016). Previous studies showed that MsrR is a cell-envelope protein from the LytR-CpsA-Psr family, which is associated with the maintenance and function of the cell-envelope and cell wall. Deletion of msrR led to changes in cell envelope and surface which caused a reduction in hydrophobicity.30,31 Although mutations in the genes pmtR, rpoB, and agrA were found in different treatment, these mutations were significantly more prevalent among Melittin populations (Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, ppmtR = 0.016, prpoB = 0.011, pagrA = 0.049). In Pexiganan populations, exclusive mutations were identified in the gene SAOUHSC_02308 (3/6; Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, p = 0.44). This gene encodes a putative membrane protein featuring PH domains. This result was not statistically significant because mutation in this gene evolved also within the Pex-Mel populations. When the test performed by grouping according to AMPs (i.e., Pex group included Pex, Pex-Temp, and Pex-Mel populations) the presence of this mutation was significantly more frequent within the Pex group (7/18 vs. 0/18, Fisher’s exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, p = 0.046). Overall, these findings suggest that while resistance to different AMPs may arise through distinct evolutionary pathways, there are some shared mutations, which can potentially contribute to either the enhancement of existing resistance or the development of primary resistance.

sec.title: Populations evolved with single AMP demonstrated higher similarity within evolutionary replicates
sec.p: In order to investigate whether populations that evolved with AMP combinations are more related to one of the treatments, both of them, or if a unique trajectory was taken, we quantify the similarity between mutation profiles using Dice similarity coefficient. A comparison of the similarities within the populations that evolved with the same treatment revealed diverse similarities (Figures S3 and S4A; permutational Kruskal-Wallis test, p = 0.012). Particularly, the populations that evolved with single AMPs showed higher similarity compared to the combination’s populations (Figure S4B; permutation test, p = 0.002). More specifically, the presence of the AMP melittin is associated with higher similarity within evolutionary replicates (Figures S3B and S4A; permutation test, p < 0.001). Among all treatments, the highest similarity was observed between Mel populations, as the average similarity was 0.52. Opposingly, within Pex-Temp populations noticed the lowest similarity (0.022). Altogether, these results suggest that for melittin there are fewer available resistance-conferring trajectories than to other AMP treatments.

sec.title: Mutations evolved under temporin-melittin exposure are similar to those that evolved under melittin alone
sec.p:
Our previous study showed that the combination of temporin-melittin was not successful in delaying resistance evolution compared with temporin alone. Although each AMP treatment yielded unique mutations, we anticipated to find shared mutations in populations exposed to a combination of two AMPs. Indeed, the similarity between Temp-Mel populations and the populations that evolved with the single AMPs was relatively high. Yet, the similarity within evolutionary replicates of Temp-Mel was not significantly different than between Temp-Mel and Mel populations (Figure 4; mean similarity of 0.2 vs. 0.26 respectively; permutation test, p = 0.26), while between Temp populations a significantly lower similarity observed (means of 0.26 vs. 0.087; permutation test, p = 0.03). Specifically, Temp-Mel populations developed pmtR and mnhD1 mutations (in at least one strain), as occurred in both single AMP populations (Figure S5). This high similarity to Mel populations was reflected by high frequency of mutations in pmtR and msrR genes (Mel: 6/6, 5/6; Temp-Mel: 4/6, 3/6, respectively). These genes also correlated with temporin and melittin resistance (Point-biserial correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, Melittin-pmtR: rpb = 0.78, p = 1.72E-06, msrR: rpb = 0.74, p = 9.75E-06; Temporin-pmtR: rpb = 0.63, p = 2.78E-03, msrR: rpb = 0.54, p = 0.016). Interestingly, msrR mutations in Mel populations were SNPs, while in the Temp-Mel populations deletion mutations evolved (Figure S2). Furthermore, the most abundant mutations in Temp populations, mnhA1 and dagK, evolved only once (mnhA1) in Temp-Mel populations. Similarly, rpoB mutations did not evolve in the combination populations but were present in most Mel evolved populations. Surprisingly, we found seven mutated genes that were exclusive to the combination treatment, with one notable gene, guaA, which evolved in 3/6 evolutionary replicates. guaA encodes a GMP-synthetase that catalyzes the synthesis of GMP from XMP. King et al. showed that the ΔguaA mutant produced an increasing amount of the antioxidant pigment staphyloxanthin.32 Our findings indicate that the guaA mutation is associated with Temp resistance (Point-biserial correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, rpb = 0.55, p = 0.016). In summary, the occurrence of the pmtR mutation across all treatments, and its ability to cf. resistance to temporin and melittin simultaneously highlights its crucial role in S. aureus resistance development toward this AMP combination.Figure 4
The internal similarity within strains exposed to the same treatment is higher than to other treatments’ populations
Dice similarity was calculated to quantify the genetic similarity between populations according to their mutation profile. Each node represents the treatment, as the percentage inside shows the mean similarity within evolutionary replicates (six populations). The lines between the nodes represent the mean similarity between those treatments’ populations. Thicker lines show higher similarity, while the asterisk determines significant difference between the internal similarity and the similarity between the different treatments’ populations. Temp- temporin; Mel-melittin; Pex-pexiganan.

sec.title: Pexiganan-temporin populations share five mutated genes with pexiganan-evolved but only one with temporin-evolved populations
sec.p: The populations that evolved with the combination of pexiganan-temporin exhibited lower resistance than each single AMP separately. Thus, we hypothesized that these populations share fewer mutated genes. The similarity analysis identified low similarity within evolutionary replicates of the combination (mean = 0.022), as well as between Pex-Temp populations and Pex and Temp populations (Figure 4). No significant difference in similarity was observed between these groups (Permutation test, pPex = 0.55, pTemp = 0.99). Although Pex and Temp populations had five overlapping mutated genes, none of them was mutated among the Pex-Temp populations (Figure S6). Furthermore, of the five genes mutated in both Pex and Pex-Temp populations, the only noteworthy gene was tagO which had two mutated populations in each treatment. Unexpectedly, despite populations with the mutated pmtR gene showing resistance to both pexiganan and temporin, the pmtR mutation, which appeared once within Temp populations and twice for Pex, did not evolve among the combination populations. Additionally, the most frequent mutation within Temp populations, in dagK, did not arise within Temp-Pex populations, which could be due to the collateral sensitivity that it confers toward pexiganan. Likewise, in Pex populations, the most common mutation, in SAOUHSC_02308 (3/6) was not observed in the combination populations. The results of this combination imply a different pathway of resistance compared with the single-AMP populations.

sec.title: The populations evolved with pexiganan-melittin exhibited mutations in a confined genetic region, particularly within the same operon
sec.p:
In the pexiganan-melittin combination we observed a significant decrease in resistance to both AMPs, compared with the populations evolved with individual AMPs.22 Hence, we assumed that the genetic profiles of each single AMP will be distinct. Surprisingly, we have found relatively high similarity between Pex and Mel evolved populations (mean = 0.159), which shared nine genes that were mutated in both treatments (Figures 5 and S7). The most frequently mutated genes, pmtR and tagO, were among these shared genes (Figure 3). Nonetheless, the mutations found in Pex-Mel populations are more similar to those found in Pex populations than in Mel populations (Figures 4 and 5; mean similarity of 0.11 vs. 0.022, respectively). Particularly, the mutation in SAOUHSC_02308, a gene which encodes for a hypothetical membrane protein featuring PH domains. Mutations in this gene appeared in 3/6 Pex populations and 4/6 Pex-Mel populations, but in none of the Mel populations (0/6). Notably, the only two Pex-Mel populations that did not evolve mutation in the mentioned gene, evolved mutation in upstream and downstream genes in the same operon (Figure S7, SAOUHSC_02307, SAOUHSC_02309). Intriguingly, all the mutations except for one (Pex3) were nonsense SNPs (stop-codon), deletion, or insertion (Figure S2). These results imply the role of this unknown membrane system in AMR, and specifically in this combination. The only gene that was mutated in both the Pex, Mel, and their combination treatment is tagO (with only one strain mutated in the combination). Consistent with the findings previously, the antimicrobial profile of the combination populations indicates medium resistance toward pexiganan but lower resistance toward melittin compared to the individual treatment (Figures 5 and S7).Figure 5
Mutations in melittin-pexiganan populations were limited to a few genes, predominantly in SAOUHSC_02308
(A) The characterization profile represents the genetic signatures and antimicrobial sensitivity properties. Each column represents a different population. Cells marked with “+” indicate mutations in specific genes. Colored cells highlight mutations found in three or more evolutionary replicates. The cross-resistance/collateral sensitivity represented in red (resistant) to blue (sensitive) scale. The table only presents mutations that occurred at least in two populations, the full table presented in Figure S7.
(B) Venn diagram of the evolved populations’ mutations illustrates the overlapping genes. Each circle shows the number of mutated genes within a treatment group, with overlaps indicating shared mutations. Mel-melittin; Pex-pexiganan; Mel-Pex- melittin-pexiganan.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The recent era of AMR has highlighted the need for alternative solutions to conventional antibiotics. AMPs, which are a natural part of the immune system in many organisms, have shown promise in addressing this issue. These peptides often coexist in diverse sets within a single species. A common example is in the skin of frogs, where numerous temporins can be found within a single organism.33 Similarly, Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) possesses seven different families of AMPs, comprising 21 associated genes.34 In humans, there are mainly two structurally distinct families: defensins and cathelicidins, with many different members inside those groups.35 Despite this, previous studies have shown that resistance to AMPs arises both in natural and laboratory settings, yet most of them examine it toward a single AMP.

While the genetic mechanism of AMP resistance has been described in several studies,10,17,36 to date, only two studies have investigated the genetic basis of resistance that arises during treatment with AMP combinations.20,21 Therefore, our study revealed the genetic profiles of AMP combination-evolved populations and compared them with populations that evolved in the presence of individual AMP. We found that S. aureus had a significantly lower number of mutations per population in the presence of two AMPs compared with single AMP treatment (Figure 1C), providing interesting insight into AMP resistance evolution. By contrast, a previous study on antibiotic combinations found no difference in the number of mutations per lineage between paired and single treatments; however, single-antibiotic evolved strains had more SNPs while the combinations-evolved strains had gene duplications more frequent.37 A possible reason for the lower number of mutations observed in combination treatments in our study is that some mutations confer resistance to one of the AMPs but increase sensitivity to another AMP. For example, we found a mutation in dagK that confers resistance to temporin but results in collateral sensitivity to pexiganan (Figure S6); Consistent with this hypothesis, the dagK mutation appeared in the Temp treatment (4/6 populations), but not in the combined Pex-Temp treatment. A similar phenomenon was reported for antibiotics.38

Although some studies have investigated the evolution of resistance to AMPs and the genetic signature of the evolved populations, knowledge of similarity of the mutations that appear in populations with the same treatment and with different treatments remains very limited. Here, we found high similarity within melittin-evolved populations, as well as within Mel combinations populations (Figure S4A). These findings suggest that the trajectory of melittin resistance is very defined, with few available resistance-conferring mutations. In contrast, pexiganan-evolved populations and Pex combinations exhibited low similarity within the populations exposed to the same treatment. Overall, combination therapy reduced the similarity within the populations with the same treatment (Figure S4B). This result supports the idea that when bacteria are exposed to two compounds simultaneously they need to acquire different mutations that potentially increase genetic diversity.

The most familiar genes involved in S. aureus AMP resistance that were reported so far, including the dlt operon and vraFG19 did not evolve in our study, whereas the mprF mutation evolved only in one population. However, we found some mutations in the genes that have already been reported. Mutation in pmtR (previously named also ytrA) which encodes for a transcriptional regulator reported in few previous studies.20,21,39 Notably, two of these studies which evolved the same strain of S. aureus with different AMPs including pexiganan and melittin found the pmtR mutation in both Mel and Pex-Mel populations, but not in Pex evolved populations.20,21 Furthermore, the same nonsense mutation that caused a stop-codon at the fifth amino acid occurred extensively in all studies. This highlights the importance of the pmtR protein in AMP resistance, and suggests that this specific point mutation confers a higher fitness, or has a higher probability of occurring.

The second most frequent mutation, tagO, was found in 10 populations; however, in contrast to pmtR, it evolved in different ways, with four missense SNPs, three insertions, two deletions, and one complex mutation. tagO (also known as tarO) is the gene encoding for the first enzyme in the WTA biosynthesis, which are anionic polymers that contribute significantly to the negative charge on the bacterial cell surface.40 A nonfunctional tagO enzyme will cause a reduction in the negative charge and thus decrease in AMP binding. Koprivnjak et al. found that tagO mutants exhibit increased resistance toward the AMP human β-defensin 3 (HBD3), which raises concerns regarding cross-resistance to human AMPs. Nevertheless, the mutant remained sensitive to another AMP, magainin 2 amide. This demonstrates the potential advantage of AMP combination therapy.24 However, the exact impact of the tagO mutations in our study is not known, as populations harbored additional mutations that may also affect AMP resistance.

The next most frequent mutation, which occurred specifically within pexiganan and Pex-Mel treatments, was found in SAOUHSC_02308 that encodes for a YdbT-like hypothetical membrane protein. This raises the hypothesis that the presence of pexiganan induces the mutation in this gene, though it was not the case in Pex-Temp combination. In the Pex-Temp combination, a low similarity was observed both within and between populations (Figure 4), suggesting the involvement of a distinct genetic pathway, as evidenced by the emergence of 12 newly mutated genes within this treatment (Figure S6). The association between mutations in SAOUHSC_02308 gene and pexiganan resistance supports this hypothesis, although not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons (Point-biserial correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, rpb = 0.47, p = 0.11). Interestingly, this hypothetical protein, containing PH domains, is extensively found in both gram-negative and gram-positive bacterial species, including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii.

Although it is widely present in many bacteria, knowledge about this protein remains limited. Perez-Ramos et al. investigated homologous proteins from Enterococcus faecalis and found that this system is used to export leaderless bacteriocin peptides, while also conferring self-immunity. In silico analysis identified significant homology of DdF protein (homology to SAOUHSC_02308) to peptidase-containing ABC transporter PCAT1 from Hungateiclostridium thermocellum.41 Another study found a similar protein, called orf8, and suggested it was involved in exporting the AMP aureocin A53 from S. aureus A53.42 A study of these proteins in Bacillus suggested that they are related to resistance to antimicrobial compounds produced by other Bacilli.43 Despite these studies, to the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to report the development of this mutation in experimental resistance evolution study.

Another prominent mutation was identified in dagK among Temp evolved populations (4/6). A spontaneously evolved mutation in this gene was reported in Lactococcus lactis, which conferred resistance toward some AMPs and other cell envelope-acting antimicrobials.44 This study showed a relatively high similarity between the DagK protein of L. lactis and S. aureus. Specifically, dagK mutation evolved only in Temp evolved populations, and not in the other treatments, including Temp combinations.

Although few of the mutations aforemented correlated with resistance to specific AMPs, testing seven available Tn-insertion mutants from the Nebraska Transposon Mutant Library (NTML) revealed that only the graS mutant showed a notable decrease in MIC value compared to the wild-type (WT) S. aureus USA300 strain (Figure S9). This result strengthens the hypothesis that AMP resistance is complex and typically requires more than mutation in a single gene to achieve high resistance.

The comparison between the combination-evolved populations’ mutational profile to each of the single-AMP-evolved populations revealed that most of the profiles of the combination populations were more similar to one of the single-AMP evolved populations, rather than showing intermediate similarity to both. Similar results have been observed for some antibiotic combinations, where resistance was lower compared to individual treatments.37 In our results, this is evident in the combination of Temp-Mel, which is largely similar to Mel populations (25% and 8.7% similarity to Mel and Temp populations, respectively). Our hypothesis is that Mel evolved populations gained mutations that provide Temp resistance, but Temp populations did not show Mel resistance comprehensively. Another example of a combination profile that is similar to one of the single-AMP evolved populations is in the combination of Pex-Mel. This combination was the most efficient in delaying the resistance occurrence when compared to individual treatment. This combination was more similar to Pex evolved populations than to Mel evolved populations (11.3% vs. 2.2%, respectively). This was an interesting combination and genetic trajectory, since both single-AMP evolved populations shared a relatively high number of overlapping mutated genes (9); however, only one of them overlapped with the Pex-Mel populations as well (tagO in one strain). Moreover, in the combination, the overall number of mutations per strain decreased significantly compared with the single-AMP populations. It seems that the mutation in the operon SAOUHSC_02307–02309 was the most beneficial and was predominant among the Pex-Mel populations. We hypothesized that these results might be caused by non-overlapping genes, i.e., genes that evolve only within one of the treatments but not in the other. Overlapping genes may cause resistance to one or both AMPs; however, when they evolved together with non-overlapping mutations, it might affect bacterial viability.

In summary, our results demonstrate that AMP resistance mechanisms tend to be complex, involving multiple genes that can differ between specific AMPs and AMP combinations. To develop significant resistance, most of the populations had to evolve more than three mutations. These results align with previous research indicating that AMP resistance, unlike antibiotic resistance, is a multi-step process involving multiple mutations and is therefore less likely to develop.45,46,47 The combination of AMP reduced the overall resistance in some cases, while the bacteria were likely to be similar to one of the signal AMP evolved populations, suggesting that AMP resistance is not general, even when the AMP combination is utilized. These findings reduce the concerns over cross-resistance of the immune system AMPs, while underscore the importance of combination therapy in AMPs. Finally, we revealed possible mechanisms of resistance in both individual and combination treatments. However, AMP combinations should be further investigated and carefully administered, as not all combinations may provide the desired effect. Moreover, our study is limited to a single S. aureus strain, and further research is needed to determine whether these findings hold across different bacterial species and strains. Our findings highlight the importance of AMP selection and combination when designing effective and druggable AMP-based therapies.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: Our study has some limitations. First, we tested only three AMPs and their combinations, representing a relatively small subset of possible AMPs. A broader selection of AMPs would help determine whether our findings are generalizable. Second, we used a single S. aureus strain (JLA513), meaning our results may differ in other S. aureus strains or bacterial species. Lastly, bacterial evolution was studied at the population level in liquid culture, but genomic DNA was extracted from a subset of this population. Consequently, low-frequency mutations may not have been detected. Future studies incorporating a more diverse range of AMPs, bacterial strains, and sequencing approaches with higher sensitivity will be necessary to refine and expand upon these findings.

sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
Bacterial strains and growth conditions
sec.p: The ancestor strain in this experiment was S. aureus JLA51348 (hla-lacZ hla1, derived from SH1000), which contains tetracycline resistance. All experiments were performed in Mueller-Hinton (MH) (HiMedia), and the bacteria were grown at 37°C. All bacterial cells used in this study were stored in 25% glycerol at -80°C.

sec.title: Experimental evolution procedure
sec.p: The experimental evolution procedure was extensively described in previously published paper.22 Prior to the evolution with AMPs, an S. aureus JLA513 colony was transferred into MH broth, grown and diluted by 20-fold for 7 consecutive days in order to habituate bacteria to the experimental conditions. After 7 transfers, 10μl from the bacterial culture (OD595=0.1) transferred into each well in a 96-well plate which contained the media and treatment compounds. The experimental protocol aimed to apply selective pressure while preventing the extinction of lines. Consequently, each line underwent exposure to 4 concentrations of AMP (in different wells) based on its MIC, specifically: 1.5x, 1x, 0.5x, and 0.25x. In this experiment, each AMP consisted of 6 parallel bacterial lines. In the AMP combination treatments, the effective ratio between the AMPs was 1:1, according to the MICs (1xMIC=0.5xMIC of each). Each plate contained positive control of bacteria only which was termed NPSA (no-peptide S. aureus), as well as negative control with media only. Rifampicin exposure was used as positive resistance control as it evolved easily.63 Every day, 10 μL from the preceding plate was replicated into 190 μL of fresh medium and AMPs, while every 4 days, bacteria that grew in the highest concentration of AMP were selected and transferred into the 4 corresponding wells in the new plate. The MIC was doubled when growth was observed in 4 out of 6 lines at the MIC or higher. The experimental evolution was continued for 29 transfers (≈122 generations). Samples were taken to glycerol stocks (25%) and preserved in -80°C before every selection to avoid line extinction.

sec.title: Genomic DNA extraction
sec.p: The glycerol stocks of bacterial populations that were preserved at the end of the experiment were inoculated into 96 deep-well plates by tip touching. The plates were shaken using a plate shaker (800 rpm) at 37°C overnight. The genomic DNA was then extracted using Bacterial Genomic DNA Isolation Kit (Norgen Biotek Corp., Thorold, Canada) according to manufacturer protocol with some modifications. In the lysate preparation the bacterial cultures were centrifuged at 4500 rcf for 5 minutes, and subsequently in the lysis process, 4μl of lysostaphin (final concentration 7.5μg/ml, Sigma-Aldrich, Merck KGaA) were added to each well.

sec.title: Whole-genome sequencing
sec.p: DNA was sequenced on an Oxford Nanopore Technologies Minion Mk1B using R10.4.1 flowcells at a translocation speed of 400 bps. Raw signal was basecalled using dorado version 0.3.049 and model ‘dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps_sup@v4.2.0'. The resulting reads were adapter-trimmed using porechop version 0.2.450 and filtered using filtlong version 0.2.151 to retain 140 Mb of reads of at least 1000 bp length. Sequencing reads were assembled using flye version 2.9.2,52 which produced a single circular 2.7-Mb contig. The assembly was polished using medaka version 1.8.053 and polypolish version 0.5.0,54 and re-circularized to begin at dnaA using circlator version 1.5.5.55 The final assembly was annotated using bakta version 1.9.3.56

Short reads were adapter-trimmed using fastp57 to a minimum length of 50 bp. Variant calling was performed by aligning reads to the reference genome using bwa version 0.7.17-r1188.58 Alignments were filtered to a minimum read mapping quality of 60 and a base quality of 13 using samtools version 1.18.59 Variants were identified using freebayes version 1.3.660 with a minimum alternate fraction 0.01 and min alternate count of 5, and filtered to a minimum quality of 100 using bcftools version 1.18.59 SnpEff version 5.061 was used to predict the effects of variants on protein-coding genes. Copy number variants were identified with cnvpytor version 1.3.1 using 1-kb bins.62 Sequencing data are available in the SRA under BioProject accession PRJNA1116739.

sec.title: Antimicrobial sensitivity of Tn-mutant strains
sec.p: Transposon insertion mutants strains provided by the Network on Antimicrobial Resistance in Staphylococcus aureus (NARSA) for distribution by BEI Resources, NIAID, NIH: Staphylococcus aureus subsp. aureus, Strain JE2 (previously known as USA300). The minimal inhibitory concentration was determined using standard MIC assay as previously described.22 Briefly, S. aureus cells were grown overnight in MH broth at 37°C with shaking at 200 rpm. The culture was then diluted 1:100 in fresh MH broth and incubated until reaching an OD595 of 0.1. Next, 100 μL of a bacterial suspension at 5 × 105 CFU/mL was added to each well of a 96-well plate containing a serial dilution of AMPs. Each AMP was tested in triplicate. The MIC was determined as the lowest concentration that inhibited bacterial growth by at least 90%. MIC fold change was calculated by dividing the mutants' MIC by the MIC of their ancestral strain (USA300).

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: All the statistical tests and results that were used in this study are reported in the statistical analysis files (Tables S3–S5). Statistical tests were performed using the Python packages scipy, scikit, sklearn. The figures were created using seaborn, matplotlib and networkx packages. Figure 1A created with Biorender.com.
